title: Sermon for the Day of the Dormition

pairs.en: *“So that your fasting will not be seen by men, but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you openly.”* [Matthew 6:18]

Today the Church brings us to stand at the graveside of the holy Virgin, and to think — with reverence. For what is a Church feast, if not exactly that: a holy meditation, in which the spirit rests from the labour of the body and gathers strength for the working days of life?

And what do we see, standing at the grave of the holy Virgin? A most unusual sight. Ordinarily there is light and clarity on *this* side of a grave, and beyond it — darkness and uncertainty. Here it is exactly the other way round. On this side of her grave: what towering excellence and virtue — wrapped in what deep mystery and obscurity! And beyond her grave: what light and glory, what a triumphant repayment of that excellence and virtue!

It takes no great effort to show that the moral worth of the most blessed Virgin Mary must be recognised as matchlessly high. It is self-evident from the dignity of the calling for which she was chosen and raised up. If a virtue higher than hers could have been found anywhere, it would have been wrong for *her*, rather than another, to be chosen to become the tabernacle, the throne, the Mother of God the Word. But in God's decisions and God's works nothing can be inconsistent. Therefore, just as surely as Mary is *“blessed among women”* [Luke 1:42] — blessed with the highest blessing, above every other woman — so surely was her virtue the highest, the purest, the most perfect; though of course she is pure and perfect through that same Christ, who Himself became the reward of her purity.
But now look how *little* of Mary's worth was known — how little of it was even visible — before her death.

Who could have known her better than the man honoured with the trust of guarding this treasure of the world, this sealed treasury of heaven? Yet Joseph, at the beginning, understood so little of the honour that was to be hers that he thought it possible she deserved public disgrace — though he was unwilling to inflict it. Joseph was ready to put away this priceless jewel; it was kept safe only because more enlightened guardians — the angels — were watching over it: *“Not willing to make her a public example, he was minded to put her away privately.* *But while he thought on these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream”* [Matthew 1:19-20].

O wondrously silent Virgin! Would it not have been more natural for you to tell Joseph yourself what an angel had to be sent to tell him at last? Why did you wait for that distant messenger from heaven? Why did you not hurry to rescue a just man who had nearly stumbled into an injustice? Without a doubt — it was so that your virtue, your grace, your dignity should *“not appear unto men,”* but only *“unto your heavenly Father, who is in secret.”*

The mystery of the Virgin Mother's high dignity was indeed partly revealed — by the angels, by the star, by the wise men of the East, by the shepherds, by the elder Simeon. But then the angels returned to heaven; the wise men went back to the East; the star disappeared; Simeon departed this world in peace; the light of Bethlehem's glory was smothered by Herod's rage and the blood of the innocent children; and Mary hid herself — now in Egypt, now in Nazareth — and buried her dignity and her glory inside her own heart: *“But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart”* [Luke 2:19].

Then came the time when the fame of the wisdom and the miracles of Mary's Son blazed through all Judea and Galilee. Surely now the reflection of the Son's glory would begin to light up the Mother as well? Once, unexpectedly, it seemed about to happen. A woman in the crowd — perhaps a mother herself, or one who longed to be — pictured more vividly than the others the happiness of the most blessed Mother, and cried out in an enthusiasm that moved her to glorify Jesus, and His Mother with Him: *“A certain woman of the company lifted up her voice and said to Him: Blessed is the womb that bore You, and the breasts that nursed You”* [Luke 11:27]. But notice — she speaks in a roundabout way. She blesses the womb; she blesses the breasts; but she never utters the *name* of the woman she is blessing. Why not? Doubtless because she does not know her — neither her face nor her name.

Others did know Mary, both by face and by name — they could hardly not know her; and yet, strangest of all, they remained ignorant of her. Listen to what the townsfolk and neighbours of Joseph and Mary say: *“Where did this Man get this wisdom, and these mighty works?”* [Matthew 13:54]. So they acknowledge the wisdom of Jesus; they see His miracles and admit them; the questions are pressing on them. And yet: *“Is not this the carpenter's son?* *Is not His mother called Mary?”* [Matthew 13:55]. Notice — they cannot even say “Joseph, the son of David; Mary, the daughter of David.” They know only the surface of things: that Joseph is a tradesman, and that Mary is — Mary. How could they not know even her family line — the one thing the Jews of that age took such care to know, about themselves and everyone else? There is only one way to explain it: the holy Virgin, wishing in no way to appear before men, seeking no human consolation, would not comfort herself in her poverty even by telling people the nobility of her royal descent. She kept her lineage as hidden as she kept her virtue and her grace.

But why be surprised that strangers — near or far — were slow to see the glory of her whom *“all generations shall call blessed”* [Luke 1:48]? Her own Son — I would hesitate to say it, if one could hesitate to repeat the words of Truth Himself — her own Son seems unwilling to give her, before men, the honour that belongs to a mother; He appears not to know her, or not to want to know her. *“Who is My mother?”* He asks [Matthew 12:48] — as though searching for someone on whom to bestow the name, the honour and the glory of “mother,” while passing over in silence the one whose childbearing had given her the right to that title. *“My mother and My brethren are these — those who hear the word of God and do it”* [Luke 8:21]. Yet in saying this, the Lord is not denying His Mother in the flesh. She hears the word of God more than anyone — she heard it before anyone; and she does it more actively than anyone — she prepared for that Word a worthy tabernacle in her own womb. No: first, the Lord is exalting all who hear and do God's word, and spurring them on in that saving work. And second, He is deliberately conforming Himself to His Mother's own rule — *not to appear before men*: standing aloof, as far as possible, from human fame, seeking only the glory that comes from God — and therefore He waits, deferring the moment when the full dignity of her who is *“more honourable than the Cherubim and more glorious than the Seraphim”* would be revealed to the world.

I walk further along the earthly road of Jesus and Mary, and everywhere I see the same. Wherever glory bursts out — Mary is absent; at the Lord's triumphant entry into Jerusalem, for instance. And where the Mother of the Lord does appear, it is never glory that meets her: *“Now there stood by the Cross of Jesus His Mother, and His Mother's sister”* [John 19:25].

Let us follow the Crucified through the door of the grave into the realm of the glory of the Risen One. The time has now come when not only the first of His disciples but even the very last in faith glorifies His divinity, crying: *“My Lord and my God!”* [John 20:28]. The glory of the resurrection is followed swiftly by the new divine glory of the Ascension. Now, at last, surely, I will find some person, some act, some word, in which the glory of *“the Mother of my Lord”* [Luke 1:43] appears — that glory which righteous Elizabeth had proclaimed at its dawn, without witnesses and without consequence. I look — and I look in vain. *“These all,”* it is written of the apostles after the Lord's Ascension, *“continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the Mother of Jesus”* [Acts 1:14]. What a strange list! Not just after the apostles — even after certain unnamed women — only then, almost as an afterthought, is *“Mary the Mother of Jesus”* remembered. What is this? Does the writer not revere the Mother of God? God keep us from a thought so offensive — offensive not only to the holy Virgin but to the holy evangelist Luke. No: it means that Luke writes the Acts of the Apostles in the very spirit in which the blessed Virgin lived among the apostles. By the height of her grace she presided, invisibly and in spirit, over that whole apostolic assembly; but by lowliness of heart she allowed herself no visible glory whatever, accepted no precedence, and set herself in the same rank as the other women — teaching them by example what the apostle Paul would later teach them in words: *“Let your women keep silence in the churches”* [1 Corinthians 14:34]; *“Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection; but I do not permit a woman to teach”* [1 Timothy 2:11-12]. I would wish — let me say it in passing — that our estranged brethren would take this example to heart: those who, ahead of Christ's own judgment, condemned the whole priesthood without distinction, punished themselves by wilfully renouncing it, and then — disorder at its height — handed the conduct of their worship over to virgins; and those virgins, surely, not wise ones but foolish [Matthew 25:2]. For what virgin, if not a foolish one, would dare to take upon herself in church what the holy Virgin, the very Mother of God, did not dare?

Now let us look at the other sphere that her assumption opened to the holy Virgin — a sphere no eye can measure, but easy to see by its sheer brightness. As soon as her falling-asleep was accomplished, the apostles — as sacred tradition tells us — were gathered from everywhere by the Holy Spirit, not so much to mourn her burial as to celebrate it. And just as once the unbelief of Thomas was turned into the very proof of Christ's resurrection, so now the *lateness* of Thomas was turned into the means of making known the taking-up of the Mother of God — until then as unrevealed as her whole life on earth had been hidden. Having received glory from God in heaven, she no longer refuses human honour on earth. Before, her humility could not welcome it; now it is useful — a blessing to those who live on earth.

Her glory, too, had its enemies — even the glory of Christ Himself had them. But here above all the divine power of grace shows itself: her enemies proved less an obstacle to her glory than an instrument of it. What did those heretics achieve, who schemed so cleverly and so boldly to strip the holy Virgin Mary of her exalted title, *Mother of God*? Only this: that the Orthodox Church, guarding against their malice, began to glorify the holy Mother of God more fervently than ever — so that now there is not one day in the Church's year, not one service, that is not richly adorned with her divine glory. And this was no mere war of words between the Orthodox and the heretics. It was a real battle between spiritual powers — and a complete victory of the power of Christ over His enemies. For the lips of those who glorify her would have grown tired over the centuries, if the holy Mother of God had not answered the voice of prayer and praise with her mighty help — bringing Christ and His grace into the soul, just as she is painted on our holy icons, carrying Him in her arms. *“Hail, thou that art highly favoured!”* [Luke 1:28] — her divine glory shines out in godlike wonders.

This, my brethren, is what I see today, standing at my post in the Church's order of service, in contemplation at the grave of the holy Virgin Mother of God. But why this vision? Because a holy meditation must not stay idle — it must become action. The example of her hidden life exists to help us understand, receive and carry out the teaching of Christ: *“…that you appear not unto men, but unto your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, shall reward you openly.”* Struggle, then; do good; serve God — but take care that your efforts, your virtues, your devotion are not paraded before men needlessly, wilfully, for self-satisfaction, for vanity. Make God the witness of your conscience, and He will be your rewarder for everything you do or suffer for His sake in secret from men.

The Lord commands secrecy, first, in works of charity: *“Take heed that you do not your alms before men, to be seen by them… when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing”* [Matthew 6:1,3]. Second, in works of devotion: *“But you, when you pray, enter into your room, and when you have shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret”* [Matthew 6:6]. Third, in works of self-denial and discipline of the body: *“…that you appear not unto men to fast, but unto your Father who is in secret.”* In other words, He commands the secrecy of modesty and lowliness in all of a person's duties — toward God, toward neighbour, toward self; in every virtue; in every work of the law.

Someone will object: then how will Christ's *other* word be fulfilled — *“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven”* [Matthew 5:16]? Do not trouble yourself over that. Christ's word will fulfil itself, without your help. It says *let* your light shine — by itself, naturally, as all light shines. It does not say: *put your light on display.* Good works are works of light in their own nature. Work in secret, and the light will shine out when, and as much as, God the Author of light commands. The only thing to fear is doing dark, evil deeds — those certainly give no light, and God will not be glorified by them.

Someone else will ask: then how is it possible to pray in church at all, or to preach, if even works of devotion must be done in secret? Remember that in the very sermon where the Saviour speaks of prayer in secret, He also speaks of the gift brought to the altar — *“if you bring your gift to the altar”* [Matthew 5:23] — and that happens only in public worship, openly and solemnly. So the command of secret prayer clearly does not release us from the duty of shared worship in church. But here too there is a prudence of its own kind: not to display yourself before men, but to stand humbly before the heavenly Father who is in secret. If, standing in church, you perform the acts of devotion that all present perform together, but strive to restrain — to make imperceptible — the private stirrings of devotion within you: the sighs and sobs that are ready to break out, the tears that are ready to flow — then even in the middle of a great assembly, you are standing before your Father *who is in secret*.

And let us reflect, brethren, how degrading, how tiring, and how useless it is to live for show — as so many do, in their moral life, their social life, their family life. They show everything, expose everything, trumpet everything; they announce every trivial act like a clucking hen announcing her new-laid egg. And the hen's announcements are the better founded! — she at least announces an egg that really exists and remains; while the vain announce things that either do not exist at all, or are destroyed by the very announcing. A deed of charity is done; very well — thus far it exists. But if the doer begins to boast of it, the good deed is annulled. It is now plain there is no goodness in his heart — only vanity reigns there. There is no goodness left in the act: the fruit of vanity is not a good deed. It is not even good in the eyes of men — for men see through vanity, and if they praise a vain man's deed, they pass sentence on his vanity in the same breath. How much less, then, is there any good in it before the eyes of God! He renounced the vain once and for all when He said: *“They have their reward”* [Matthew 6:2].

Christian! **Be — and do not seem.** That is one of the most important rules you will ever receive. Learn the incomparable dignity of modest, quiet, hidden virtue. It is the nature of such virtue to be a mystery on earth, because it is born of heaven and exists for heaven. Perfect it in secret; guard it from the eyes of men — eyes so often impure, which stain its purity; and offer it, fervently and without ceasing, to the pure and purifying eye of God. *“And your Father, who sees in secret, shall Himself reward you openly.”* Amen.
